content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose to modify the last layer of a classification network by introducing a Nadaraya-Watson head, which estimates the probability of belonging a class by checking how close the input data deep features are with respect to a predefined support set. In essence, it works similar to a neural network attached to a SVM-RBF kernel, with the particularity that they are trained at the same time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* The idea is easy to understand and to implement.
* The explainable mechanism  provide some insights about the decision making.

Weaknesses
* The computational cost can be extremely high when using the full dataset as support set.
* It is not clear how and when the support set is selected when using k-means versions.
* The idea is very similar to a deep feature mechanism followed by a svm-rbf classifier.
* The experimental results are not impressive.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
* The idea is easy to understand and to implement.
* However, it is not clear how the support set is selected when using k-means versions. Does it change as the g() network is updated?

Quality
* The experimental results shows no big gain with respect to the classic DL classification approach. 
* It is also only tested using one type of architecture (ResNet), which makes it difficult to generalize the results to any other solution.
* The idea of using a sample batch for the support kernel is very interesting, as it can speed up the process by a huge margin. However, it is not clear how the tradeoff between $N_s$ and $N_b$ can affect the results. An ablation study regarding this point should be included.
* Regarding to the explainable mechanism, one can argue that this same solution can be applied to the deep features related to a classic DL approach. A comparison (it could be merely visual) between the results obtained by either features should be included.

Novelty
* The idea is very similar to the so-called Radial Basis Function Networks (RBFS) [1, 2], although the introduction of the support set batch is an interesting idea that is advisable to pursue.

Reproducibility
* Besides the confusion regarding to how the support set is selected, the contribution provides enough elements to successfully reproduce the paper results

[1] Ghosh, J., & Nag, A. (2001). An overview of radial basis function networks. Radial Basis Function Networks 2, 1-36.

[2]. Zhang, D., Zhang, N., Ye, N., Fang, J., & Han, X. (2020). Hybrid learning algorithm of radial basis function networks for reliability analysis. IEEE Transactions on reliability, 70(3), 887-900.

content.title: Response to reviewer GHtA, 1/2
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer GHtA for helpful feedback on our work. We address many of Reviewer GHtA’s suggestions in the general response above and respond to specific comments below.

> The computational cost can be extremely high when using the full dataset as support set.

We agree with the reviewer that full dataset evaluation can be computationally expensive (as much as 2x inference time in our experiments). In our paper, we explore several inference modes which each have advantages and trade-offs. In particular, we find that Cluster mode can be a sufficient replacement to Full mode (Figure 2), while being computationally cheaper (Table 2). Nevertheless, Full mode allows user practitioners to interpret and debug a model’s behavior (Section 4.3). Thus, one can imagine a workflow for the practitioner which would involve using Cluster mode to perform efficient inference, and then turning to Full mode on a select few (potentially problematic) test queries to understand model behavior. We stress that this flexibility at inference time is not possible with FC baseline models. 

> It is not clear how and when the support set is selected when using k-means versions.

For Cluster mode, we first compute all embeddings for the dataset. Subsequently, for each class, we collect the embeddings for that class and perform k-means clustering on these class-specific embeddings. The resulting $k$ centroids are the support embeddings used during inference, where $k$ corresponds to the number of support embeddings per class (e.g. the x-axis value in Figure 2). 

For Closest cluster mode, we compute the embeddings in the same way as Cluster mode, but instead of using those embeddings directly, we use the embeddings closest to the centroids in the training dataset. These embeddings thus correspond to real images in the training set, and can be interpreted and visualized (see Figure 3).

Note that computing clusters can be done offline - thus, this does not affect time for inference at deployment. We have added this further clarification in the revised manuscript.

> The idea is very similar to a deep feature mechanism followed by a svm-rbf classifier. 

Unlike an SVM, we do not formulate the classification problem as one of finding a (set of) linearly separating hyperplane(s). Instead, our formulation is more similar to a “soft” nearest-neighbors, where the label of a given query datapoint is computed as a weighted sum of labels of neighboring datapoints.

> The idea is very similar to the so-called Radial Basis Function Networks (RBFS) [1, 2], although the introduction of the support set batch is an interesting idea that is advisable to pursue.

Thank you for pointing out this relevant work - we have added these references to our paper. An RBFS is a parametric network parameterized by a weighted sum of RBFs (kernels), with an additional bias term. One notable difference between our method and RBFSs is that we do not learn the RBF centers as part of the optimization process. Instead, our model is based on the nonparametric Nadaraya-Watson estimator, in which the “kernels'' are computed with respect to real datapoints in a support set. This nonparametric property implies that the capacity of the model is tied to the number of datapoints in the support set (see, e.g., Figure 2). Nevertheless, to your point, future work may explore learning this support set, in a manner similar to RBFSs.

>The experimental results are not impressive. The experimental results shows no big gain with respect to the classic DL classification approach.

From Figure 2 and Table 1, we observe an average of +7% accuracy improvement and nearly an order of magnitude calibration improvement across the 4 datasets we tested. We believe that this is a significant improvement, especially given the relatively simple change (FC head to NW head). In addition, this change opens the door for interpretability and explainability (Section 4.3) and flexibility in designing the support set at inference time, which are all not possible with the baseline FC head.

> It is also only tested using one type of architecture (ResNet), which makes it difficult to generalize the results to any other solution.

In our experiments, we experimented with two architectures, ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121 (see, e.g. Table 1). We find that our calibration (and to a lesser extent, accuracy) improvements hold across both architectures.

content.title: Response to reviewer GHtA, 2/2
content.comment:
> The idea of using a sample batch for the support kernel is very interesting, as it can speed up the process by a huge margin. However, it is not clear how the tradeoff between $N_s$ and $N_b$ can affect the results. An ablation study regarding this point should be included.

Thank you for this suggestion. Prompted by this, we conducted an experiment on the Bird dataset where we varied the hyperparameters $(N_b, N_s)$ such that the total number of images per mini-batch is constant: 

| $(N_b, N_s)$ | Accuracy |
| ----------- | ----------- |
| (1, 40)| 0.45     |
| (2, 20)| 0.49     |
| (4, 10)| 0.53     |
| (5, 8)| 0.53    |
| (8, 5)| 0.52     |
| (10, 4)| 0.49     |
| (20, 2)| 0.42     |


We find that there is a sweet spot around (4,10) and (5,8). We hypothesize that low batch size $N_b$ hurts convergence, as is typical for SGD optimization. On the other hand, low $N_s$ may be non-ideal because the model does not have sufficient number of “negative” samples to compare against. With that said, the performance is not particularly sensitive with respect to reasonable values of $N_s$. We believe that balancing this tradeoff is important to maximizing performance on a given dataset. We will highlight this observation in our revision.

> Regarding to the explainable mechanism, one can argue that this same solution can be applied to the deep features related to a classic DL approach. A comparison (it could be merely visual) between the results obtained by either features should be included.

Thank you for this suggestion. Prompted by this, we have added an additional figure in Appendix A.4 which visualizes the closest images to the query image in the feature space for the FC model. One can compare this to the same queries visualized in Appendix A.3. In general, we find that the degree of subjectively assessed semantic similarity between the query and the top images is much higher for the NW head. This is likely due to the fact that feature-wise similarity is explicitly enforced in the NW head, whereas the FC head only needs to learn features which can be separated by hyperplanes. There is no guarantee that distance in feature space is tied to visual similarity in the FC head.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new output layer for deep neural networks (DNNs) called Nadaraya-Watson (NW) head.
NW head essentially computes Nadaraya-Watson regression given an input feature and a support set (a set of features and their outcomes).
The authors reported that NW head have some useful properties such as (i) the classification results tend to be calibrated compared to standard fully connected layer, (ii) a variant of influence function called support influence can be computed efficiently, and (iii) one can obtain relevant support instances for interpreting the outcome of DNN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
The idea of using NW head instead of fully connected layer will be reasonable.
In particular, as the authors claimed, one can naturally obtain instance-based interpretation from the NW head.
The reported results well demonstrate that the obtained instance-based interpretations look intuitive and reasonable.

### Weakness
#### Weakness1
The essential weakness of the paper is on the novelty of the NW head.
As the authors mentioned in the related work, NW-type layers are typically used in the context of few-shot classification.
That is, the NW head itself will not be novel.
The true novelty of the paper will be on identifying some of its practical utilities in standard learning problems.
The current writing of the paper, in particular Introduction, looks misleading as if NW head itself is novel.
It would be more appropriate to position the NW head as the known layer, and puts the emphasis of the paper on its practical utilities.

#### Weakness2
There is also a question on the utility of the NW head (also see Weakness3 below).
In Sec4.3.1, the authors demonstrated that the NW head can provide a few instances as the supporting evidences for the outcome of DNN.
My point here is that this is not the unique utility of the NW head.
Indeed, sorting the contributions by the weight $w(x, x_s)$ is equivalent to sorting by the distance $\|g(x) - g(x_s)\|$.
Apparently, this is possible for any DNNs if we pick an appropriate layer as $g$.
If we look into [Ref1] who provided an exhaustive comparisons of instance similarities, it is reported that the L2 distance in the last layer of DNN can provide similar instances of the same class, showing DNNs without the NW head can do something similar as in Sec4.3.1.

* [Ref1] Evaluation of Similarity-based Explanations, ICLR'21.

#### Weakness3
Another question on the utility of the NW head is on support influence.
Again, this may not be the unique utility of the NW head.
If I understand correctly, the instances considered as influential by the support influence is essentially the ones $(x_s, y_s)$ close to $x$ whose label is different from the majority of the instances around $x$.
We can find such points for any DNNs even without the NW head.

Formally, according to the definition of the NW head (5) and the support influence (8), the influential instances need to be the ones that have large difference $f(x, \mathcal{S}) - f(x, \mathcal{S}_{-z_s})$; otherwise, the support influence must be small.
With some calculous, we can find that the difference can be rearranged as follows.

$$f(x, \mathcal{S}) - f(x, \mathcal{S}_{-z_s})$$

$$
= \frac{\exp\left(- \|g(x) - g(x_s)\|^2\right) }{\sum_{j \neq s} \exp\left(- \|g(x) - g(x_j)\|^2\right)} \frac{\sum_{j = 1}^{N_s} \exp\left(- \|g(x) - g(x_j)\|^2\right) (y_s - y_j) }{\sum_{j=1}^{N_s} \exp\left(- \|g(x) - g(x_j)\|^2\right)} .
$$

The first term of the right hand side measures the closenss of $x_s$ to $x$, relative to the other instances.
That is, the point $x_s$ close to $x$ is the candidate of influential instances.
The second term of the right hand side measures the discrepancy between $y_s$ and the labels of the instances close to $x$.
The magnitude of this term gets large when $y_s$ is different from the majority of instances around $x$.
From these two terms, we find that the influential instances are the ones $(x_s, y_s)$ close to $x$ whose label is different from the other instances around $x$.

#### Suggestion for Weakness2, 3
The current paper shows the capability of the NW head that it can provide supporting evidences as well as influential instances.
However, as I pointed out above, this may not be a unique property of the NW head, and we can compute similar stuffs for general DNNs.
It is therefore essential to show not only the capability of the NW head but also its superiority over general DNNs without the NW head.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
#### Clarity
The paper is written clearly and the main claim is easy to follow.
However, as I pointed out in Weakness1, some parts of the paper looks misleading as if NW head itself is novel.

#### Quality, Novelty
As I pointed out in Weakness1, the NW head itself will not be novel.
It would be more appropriate to position the NW head as the known layer, and puts the emphasis of the paper on its practical utilities.

However, some of the practical utilities claimed in the paper are also in question.
As I pointed out in Weakness2, 3, it will be possible to obtain similar results from DNNs even without the NW head.
For example, [Ref1] reported that the L2 distance in the last layer of DNN can provide similar instances of the same class, showing DNNs without the NW head can do something similar as the NW head.
It would be therefore essential to show not only the capability of the NW head but also its superiority over general DNNs without the NW head.

#### Reproducibility
The experimental setups are described in the paper.
The results will be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think the use of the NW head will be an interesting choice for interpretable DNNs.
However, its novelty and some of its practical utilities claimed in the paper are questionable.
The NW head itself seems to a known component, and some of its utilities claimed in the paper can be realized even for general DNNs without the NW head.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to reviewer dLVq
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer dLVq for helpful feedback on our work. We address many of Reviewer dLVq’s suggestions in the general response above and respond to specific comments below.

> Weakness1. The essential weakness of the paper is on the novelty of the NW head...

Thank you for pointing this out. We would like to stress that, while similar ideas have been proposed in the context of few-shot classification, we are the first to propose using a deep feature extractor followed by an NW head in the standard classification setting, to the best of our knowledge. Our experiments show that the simple change that this head represents can lead to slightly improved accuracy and (sometimes dramatically) improved calibration, which is a novel finding. We also believe that the inference modes we propose are novel and showcase the flexibility and choice that a user practitioner has in interfacing with the NW head, whether for the end purpose of interpretability, explainability, computational efficiency, or performance.

> Weakness2. There is also a question on the utility of the NW head (also see Weakness3 below)...

Thank you for this suggestion - we have added this related work to our paper. Prompted by this, we have added an additional figure in Appendix A.4 which visualizes the closest images to the query image in the feature space for the FC model. One can compare this to the same queries visualized in Appendix A.3. In general, we find that the degree of visual similarity between the query and the top most similar images is much higher for the NW head. This is likely due to the fact that feature-wise similarity is explicitly enforced in the NW head, whereas the FC head only needs to learn features which can be separated by hyperplanes. There is no guarantee that distance in feature space is tied to visual similarity in the FC head.

> Weakness3. Another question on the utility of the NW head is on support influence...

Thank you for your comment on the influence function. Your derivation does not exactly follow our definition (change in loss function and not predicted probabilities). As we show below, however, the ranking of helpful/harmful examples based on the influence function is indeed equivalent to simply ranking by the weights for correct and incorrect classes. We believe that this intuitive interpretation reveals an interesting connection between the weights in the NW head and the definition of the influence function in the robust statistics literature.


Let us start from the definition of support influence in Eq. 8:

$\mathcal{I}(z, z_s) = L(f(x,\mathcal{S} \setminus {z_s}), y) - L(f(x, \mathcal{S}), y) = \log\left( \frac{f^{y} - f^{y}w(x, x_s)}{f^{y} - w(x, x_s) {1}_{\{y = y_s\}}} \right),$

where $0 \leq w \leq f^y \leq 1$.
Note that $w \leq f^y$ because they are related by Eq. 3:
\begin{equation}
    f(x, \mathcal{S}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} w(x, x_i) \vec{y}_i.
\end{equation}

Separate into two cases:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}(z, z_s) = \begin{cases}
    \log\left(\frac{1 - w(x, x_s)}{1 - w(x, x_s)/f^y}\right), &\text{if} \ y = y_s \\\\
    \log({1 - w(x, x_s)}), &\text{else}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

In the first case where $y=y_s$, $\mathcal{I}(z, z_s)$ increases as $w$ increases, with the constraints on $w$ and $f^y$.

In the second case where $y \neq y_s$, $\mathcal{I}(z, z_s)$ decreases as $w$ increases.

In words, the support influence increases as the weight increases for the correct class, and decreases as the weight increases for the incorrect class. Thus, the support influence can be interpreted as simply ranking by the weights for correct and incorrect classes.

We have added this explanation and analysis in the main text and the Appendix.

content.title: Thank you for reply
content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for the detailed replay.

> Weakness1. The essential weakness of the paper is on the novelty of the NW head...

I am happy if the authors read my comment more carefuly.
I have never denied the utility of the NW head that the authors mentioned in the reply.

> The true novelty of the paper will be on identifying some of its practical utilities in standard learning problems. ... It would be more appropriate to position the NW head as the known layer, and puts the emphasis of the paper on its practical utilities.

My point here is how the novely of the NW head is described in the paper. As I commented in my review, my only concern is that "The current writing of the paper, in particular Introduction, looks misleading as if NW head itself is novel." To my knowledge, the NW-like architecture is already used in some of the deep models such as in few-shot learning (+ NW is sometimes discussed with its similarity to attention ). 

> Weakness2. There is also a question on the utility of the NW head ...

I would like to thank the authors for adding the results on the Euclidean distance on DNNs with FC layers.
I confirm that the Euclidean distance seems to fail on the second bird in Figure 13. 
However, I do not find so much difference on the other examples, which raises a question on claiming the validity based solely on subjective evaluation on visual similairty.
For example, one can easily claim that the NW head may not be working appropriately by raising the third flower in Figure 9, where, to me, the Euclidean distance looks it is doing better job in Figure 14.

> Weakness3. Another question on the utility of the NW head is on support influence...

My comment in the review aims at understanding the meaning of support influence in general deep models.
I understand that my derivation does not exactly follows how the suport influence is introduced in the paper, where my derivation can still be interpreted as the necessary condition for support influence (i.e., the derived difference must be large for influenctial instances).
And, I found that the influential instances are necessary to be the ones $(x_s, y_s)$ close to $x$ whose label is different from the other instances around $x$.
This interpretation allows us to compute something similar to support influence (even though it is not completely identical) for general deep models.
This is the reason why I pointed that "support influence" may not be a unique property of the NW head.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4362 by Reviewer Y7mf

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers the problem of achieving better calibration and explainability for classification using deep learning.
The method is simple: the fully-connected head is replaced with a "Nadaraya-Watson" head that acts similarly to attention.
Predictions take the form of a convex combination of the (one-hot) labels of examples in a support set, with weights determined by a softmax-normalized distance in feature space.
During training, the support set is randomly sampled; during testing, the support set may be the training set or a representative set of samples obtained by clustering.
The form of the prediction enables a closed-form expression for the influence of each support example on the prediction, which is useful for debugging incorrect predictions.
An empirical study is conducted with 4 small-medium datasets for image classification.
The proposed method is shown to achieve comparable accuracy and superior calibration compared to a fully-connected baseline.
Results improve as the size of the support set increases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. The paper is well written and easy to read.
1. The method achieves comparable accuracy and significantly better calibration.
1. While nearest neighbors have been visualized before, this method describes how each neighbor directly affects the prediction.
1. The explainability visualizations in Figures 5 and 6 are striking and indeed seem useful.
1. Similarly, the diversity shown by the cluster centroids in Figure 3 is nice.
1. One strength which did not seem to be noted in the paper is that the method achieves significantly lower validation loss than FC! (Figure 2 and Appendix A.3)

**Weaknesses**

1. The datasets seem relatively small, especially given the high capacity of the networks (ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121). Perhaps this high capacity leads to worse overfitting with the FC head. It remains to be seen whether the findings would generalize to a large-scale dataset like ImageNet.

1. There is no comparison to other techniques that can improve calibration, such as label smoothing, temperature scaling, focal loss, mixup, splines.

1. The curves in Figure 2 (and Appendix A.3) look quite noisy. It would be preferable to conduct multiple trials and plot the average, along with confidence intervals.

1. Is there a difference between using the influence metric and simply ranking examples by similarity within correct/incorrect classes? Perhaps the magnitude of the influence metric is informative?

1. Possibly limited novelty and missing references, see below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

Excellent.

**Reproducibility**

I believe there is sufficient information to reproduce the results.
The code will be made available.

* Were the models trained from scratch or initialised from a checkpoint?

**Quality**

The ideas and empirical investigation appear sound. The experiments would benefit from averaging over multiple trials. The datasets may be small compared to the model size.

**Novelty**

The method is surprisingly simple, so the novelty is somewhat limited.
However, I believe that it has not previously been investigated as a technique for obtaining better calibration, and it seems quite effective.

It may be worth including these references, which use a similar formulation, although not for the purpose of achieving well-calibrated confidences:
* Laenen and Bertinetto, 2021, "On Episodes, Prototypical Networks, and Few-Shot Learning"
* Iscen et al. 2022, "Learning with Neighbor Consistency for Noisy Labels"
* Frosst et al., 2019, "Analyzing and improving representations with the soft nearest neighbor loss"
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is well written and shows that a simple but elegant method improves calibration and provides direct explainability.
The paper would have been strengthened by conducting an experiment with a larger dataset and comparing against other techniques for improving calibration.
I'm leaning towards accept but I may downgrade my rating if the other reviewers have similar concerns and they cannot be addressed in the rebuttal.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4362 by Reviewer Y7mf

content.title: Response to reviewer Y7mf
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer Y7mf for positive comments and helpful feedback on our work. We address many of Reviewer Y7mf’s suggestions in the general response above and respond to specific comments below.

> The datasets seem relatively small, especially given the high capacity of the networks (ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121). Perhaps this high capacity leads to worse overfitting with the FC head. It remains to be seen whether the findings would generalize to a large-scale dataset like ImageNet.

Prompted by this comment, we have added clarification in our Experiment section, stating that the evidence we provide in the Experiments section suggests that our method offers gains over FC head in small-medium sized datasets and with relatively fine-grained labels. We agree with the reviewer that exploring the advantages/drawbacks of the NW head in diverse datasets like ImageNet remains an important future work.

> There is no comparison to other techniques that can improve calibration, such as label smoothing, temperature scaling, focal loss, mixup, splines.

Thank you for the suggestion. Note that although our method exhibits improved calibration, we do not specifically target calibration in our architecture; indeed, the NW head is orthogonal to these calibration techniques. To explore these ideas,  we experimented with two popular techniques for improving calibration, label smoothing (LS) and temperature scaling (TS), and present these new results in Table 3, for both FC and NW heads. 

In general, we find that our method outperforms the FC method under both LS and TS techniques. In particular, the post-training technique of TS is a simple strategy that further improves our calibration performance.

> The curves in Figure 2 (and Appendix A.3) look quite noisy. It would be preferable to conduct multiple trials and plot the average, along with confidence intervals.

Thank you for this suggestion. We have run 3 trials of each of the models with 3 separate seeds and added them to Figure 2. In general, we notice significantly smoother curves.

> Is there a difference between using the influence metric and simply ranking examples by similarity within correct/incorrect classes? Perhaps the magnitude of the influence metric is informative?


Thank you for this comment. Prompted by this, we provide a derivation below that shows that ranking by helpful/harmful examples is indeed equivalent to simply ranking by the weights for correct and incorrect classes. We believe that this intuitive explanation for the behavior of the support influence represents an interesting connection between the NW head and the definition of the influence function in the robust statistics literature.

Let us start from the definition of support influence in Eq. 8:

$\mathcal{I}(z, z_s) = L(f(x,\mathcal{S} \setminus {z_s}), y) - L(f(x, \mathcal{S}), y) = \log\left( \frac{f^{y} - f^{y}w(x, x_s)}{f^{y} - w(x, x_s) {1}_{\{y = y_s\}}} \right),$

where $0 \leq w \leq f^y \leq 1$.
Note that $w \leq f^y$ because they are related by Eq. 3:
\begin{equation}
    f(x, \mathcal{S}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_s} w(x, x_i) \vec{y}_i.
\end{equation}

Separate into two cases:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}(z, z_s) = \begin{cases}
    \log\left(\frac{1 - w(x, x_s)}{1 - w(x, x_s)/f^y}\right), &\text{if} \ y = y_s \\\\
    \log({1 - w(x, x_s)}), &\text{else}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

In the first case where $y=y_s$, $\mathcal{I}(z, z_s)$ increases as $w$ increases, with the constraints on $w$ and $f^y$.

In the second case where $y \neq y_s$, $\mathcal{I}(z, z_s)$ decreases as $w$ increases.

In words, the support influence increases as the weight increases for the correct class, and decreases as the weight increases for the incorrect class. Thus, the support influence can be interpreted as simply ranking by the weights for correct and incorrect classes.

We have added this explanation and analysis in the main text and the Appendix.

> Possibly limited novelty and missing references, see below.

Thank you for the references - we have added them to our paper. We hope that the previous and newly added results reinforce our main message that our simple change can lead to (perhaps surprisingly) improved calibration and interpretability/explainability capabilities.

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive review of our manuscript. In response to feedback, we provide a general response here to points raised by multiple reviewers, and provide reviewer-specific, point-by-point responses below.

Regarding concerns from reviewers about novelty, we emphasize that the three key contributions of this work are:

1. Designing a nonparametric Nadaraya-Watson (NW) image classification head that relies on a support set, which lends itself to being interpretable and well-calibrated. Prior works which use an NW-like setup [1] do not consider the image classification task nor explore the interpretability/calibration advantages it offers. 
2. Proposing multiple inference “modes'' corresponding to different choices of the support set at test-time. This provides a degree of flexibility not possible with baseline classifiers with a fully-connected (FC) head.
3. Deriving an easy-to-compute influence function for the NW head. Prior work on applying influence functions to deep networks for explainability [2] requires approximations and cannot be computed in closed form.

In response to reviewers Y7mf and Trz4 asking about baseline methods for calibration, we have added an additional experiment in Table 3, where we explore two popular and effective calibration techniques: label smoothing (LS) [3] and temperature scaling (TS) [4]. Since the NW head is a general purpose image classification model, we can apply LS and TS to it as well as to the FC head. We find that these techniques can improve the already well-calibrated predictions from the NW head, and furthermore that these techniques generally outperform the FC head.

Reviewers Y7mf and dLVq asked whether the helpful/harmful support images derived from the support influence is equivalent to ranking by weight within correct and incorrect classes. We provide mathematical analysis that this is true in A.2. We believe that this intuitive explanation for the behavior of the support influence represents an interesting connection between the NW head and the definition of the influence function in the robust statistics literature.

In response to reviewers dLVq and GHtA asking about whether ranking features according to distance in feature space for parametric models can achieve the same effect as our nonparametric setup, we have added an additional set of figures in Appendix A.4. These figures visualize the closest images to the query image in the feature space for the FC model. One can compare this to the same queries visualized in Appendix A.3. In general, we find that the degree of visual similarity between the query and the top most similar images is much higher for the NW head. This is likely due to the fact that feature-wise similarity is explicitly enforced in the NW head, whereas the FC head only needs to learn features which can be separated by hyperplanes. There is no guarantee that distance in feature space is tied to visual similarity in the FC head.

Other minor changes:

1. Fixed issue with weight visualizations (e.g. Fig. 5) where ordering was in column-major order instead of row-major order.

2. Show reliability diagram for one architecture in main text and put the other in Appendix, to fit the page limit.

[1] Vinyals et al. Matching networks for one shot learning, 2016.

[2] Koh et al. Understanding black-box predictions via influence functions, 2017.

[3] Szegedy et al. Rethinking the inception architecture for computer vision, 2015

[4] Guo et al. On calibration of modern neural networks, 2017.
